description: Selectors, properties, and the three ways to attach styles to a page.

screens.body:
HTML builds the house: walls, rooms, doors. CSS is the paint, the wallpaper, the curtains — everything about how it looks.

Without CSS, every page would be plain black text on a white background. CSS lets you set colors, sizes, spacing, fonts, and layouts.

The good news: CSS is built from a few small building blocks, and they combine into everything you see on styled websites.
screens.heading: CSS is the paint job
screens.keyPoint: HTML = structure. CSS = how it looks.

screens.body:
A CSS rule starts with a selector — the part that says WHICH elements to style.

p targets every paragraph. .note targets every element with class="note" (dot = class). #hero targets the one element with id="hero" (hash = id).

Think of it like addressing a letter: the selector is the name on the envelope.

code.snippet:
p { color: gray; }      /* every paragraph */
.note { color: blue; } /* class="note" */
#hero { color: red; }  /* id="hero" */

screens.heading: Selectors pick your targets

screens.body:
After the selector come curly braces filled with declarations: property: value; pairs.

color: blue; sets the text color. font-size: 20px; sets the size. Each declaration ends with a semicolon — forget one and the next declaration breaks.

One rule can hold as many declarations as you like. The braces hold the whole rule together.

screens.heading: Three ways to attach CSS
screens.keyPoint: Separate file = cleanest. Inline = last resort.

screens.body:
color sets the text color; background-color paints behind the text. Use color names (purple), hex codes (#7b2ff7), or rgb(123, 47, 247) — they all work.

font-size controls size, font-weight controls boldness (normal, bold, or numbers like 700), and text-align lines text up left, center, or right.

Small combos go a long way: a colored heading with centered text already looks designed.
screens.heading: Colors and text
screens.keyPoint: color, background-color, font-size, text-align do most of the work.

screens.body:
An element selector (p) styles EVERY paragraph. A class (.btn) styles only the elements wearing it — and you can reuse it anywhere.

One element can wear several classes: <button class="btn btn-big"> gets both styles. Name classes by their role (btn-primary), not their look (blue-btn) — looks change.

That's why classes are the workhorse of real CSS: define once, reuse everywhere.

check.question: An element has class="btn big". Which selectors style it?

screens.heading: Classes are reusable outfits

screens.body:
px = pixels, an exact size: font-size: 16px. Simple and predictable.

% = relative to the parent: width: 50% means half the parent's width. Great for layouts that stretch.

em and rem scale with font size — rem is based on the page's root size, so rem-based spacing grows nicely when users zoom. You'll see them everywhere in real code.
